Grade Band B (Grades 6–8) scaffold. This page is pinned in every module so a scholar who enrolls mid-year can find it without asking the teacher.

1 · How to Sign In

Go to office.com and sign in with your school Microsoft account (not a personal Microsoft account). Your username is your Optima email address. If you don't know your password, contact your teacher.

2 · This Course's OneDrive Folder

Create (or confirm you already have) this folder path in OneDrive: Optima → Civics → Civics_2026-27. Save every Word or PowerPoint file for this course there.

3 · File Naming Rule

Every file you submit follows this pattern: LastName_FirstName_AssignmentShortName_CIV8_2627

Example: Reed_Patrick_LockeAnalysis_CIV8_2627. Multi-draft assignments add _Draft1, _Draft2, or _Final.

4 · How to Submit via Canvas

Open the assignment in Canvas. If it uses the OneDrive cloud-assignment tool, your personal copy opens automatically; complete it and click Submit in Canvas when done. If it's a file-upload assignment, use the OneDrive tab in the submission window to attach your saved file directly; don't download-then-reupload.

  1. Confirm you have a school M365 account. If not, contact your teacher.
  2. Create your Optima → Civics → Civics_2026-27 OneDrive folder if it doesn't exist yet.
  3. Review the file naming rule above and bookmark this page.
  4. Ask your teacher whether any earlier assignments need to be made up in M365 format.

Ask your teacher first. For Microsoft's own beginner tutorials, visit support.microsoft.com.

assignments.title: 1.7 Critical Questions
assignments.html:
Reread Primary Source 1 (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians, ch. 21), including the translation note, then read it in the context of Lesson 1.1 before answering. Your answers should reason from the text, not just restate it.

  1. This passage is really an argument about what makes someone a full member of the political community. Based on the passage and Lesson 1.1, was Cleisthenes's central achievement here extending the vote to people who lacked it, or extending citizenship itself to people who had never held it? Explain the difference and defend your answer.
  2. Suppose Cleisthenes had kept the old four tribes but simply given commoners the right to address the Assembly, without creating any new tribes at all. Would recent immigrants outside the four traditional tribes have gained citizenship this way? Why or why not?

assignments.title: 1.11 Primary Source Report
assignments.html:
M365 Skill Step (Grade Band B, Module 1: full instruction). This is the first written Report of the course. Before submitting: open Microsoft Word from your school M365 account; name your file LastName_FirstName_PSReport1_CIV8_2627; save it to Optima -> Civics -> Civics_2026-27 in OneDrive; submit through Canvas using the OneDrive tab. M365 Skill You're Practicing: Applying Heading Styles (Word). Use a Heading 1 style for your name/title and Heading 2 styles for each numbered response.

Write a short Word document (250-400 words total) answering the following. Quote directly from both primary sources at least once each.

  1. Plutarch says Solon deliberately wrote vague laws so that popular courts, not the letter of the law, would settle disputes. Why might a reformer trying to expand ordinary people's power actually want the law to be unclear? What does this suggest about where Solon believed legitimate authority ultimately rested?
  2. If Cleisthenes had never broken up the old tribes, could Solon's system of courts and juries alone have produced a stable democracy? Defend your answer using both sources.

assignments.title: 1.12 VR A: Walking the Athenian Agora
assignments.html:
Setting: the Athenian Agora. Time: ~20 minutes. Feeds: Module 1 background knowledge.

Enter the virtual reconstruction of the Athenian Agora. A note at the starting point marks three stops: the Bouleuterion (Council house), the law courts, and the ostracism voting area. At each stop, read the posted placard describing the building's function, then leave your own note answering: 'Who would have used this building, and for what?' Before you finish, use the drawing tool or a whiteboard to sketch the basic layout connecting all three stops, and record a walkthrough of your finished sketch as you narrate a one-sentence summary of how the three buildings worked together.

Submit: the recording of your walkthrough, uploaded here.

Facilitator note: Students commonly confuse the Bouleuterion (Council of 500) with the full Assembly meeting place (the Pnyx, visited in VR 1B). Have the terminology guide handy if a student asks the difference.

assignments.title: 1.13 VR B: The Pnyx, A Citizen's-Eye View of the Assembly
assignments.html:
Setting: Pnyx Hill. Time: ~20 minutes. Feeds: Module 1 background knowledge.

Enter the virtual reconstruction of Pnyx Hill. You will begin on the speaker's platform (the bema) looking out over the space where up to 6,000 citizens gathered to vote directly on the city's laws. Read the pre-placed whiteboard summarizing three real motions the Assembly once debated. Choose one, and using a note, write the argument you would have made for or against it if you had been a citizen standing in the crowd. Then walk to where the crowd would have stood and record a short walkthrough narrating why direct democracy felt different from the ten-tribe reform you studied in Lesson 1.2.

Submit: the recording of your walkthrough, uploaded here.

Facilitator note: Some students expect a 'vote' mechanic in-world; there isn't one. The point is spatial perspective-taking, not a simulation. Redirect students toward the writing/recording task if they get stuck looking for an interactive vote.

assignments.title: 1.17 Critical Questions
assignments.html:
Reread the Cicero excerpt above, then read it in the context of Lesson 2.1 before answering. Your answers should reason from the text, not just restate it.

  1. Cicero's definition implies that a group of people gathered by force, without shared agreement about justice, would not count as a genuine "people" or commonwealth at all. What would this imply about a kingdom ruled purely by fear? Is it a "res publica" by Cicero's definition?
  2. Suppose Rome had never developed the office of Tribune of the Plebs, and the plebeians had no institutional voice at all. Could Cicero still call Rome's government a res publica, "the property of a people," under his own definition? Why or why not?

assignments.title: 1.20 Primary Source Exercise
assignments.html:
Reread the Polybius excerpt above, then read it in the context of Lesson 2.2 before answering.

  1. Polybius is applying a Greek theoretical framework (the three good forms and their three corrupt twins) to a Roman reality that does not fit any one category cleanly. What does this tell you about the difference between a government's formal design and how a political theorist classifies it?
  2. If Rome had abolished the office of consul and given all executive power to the Senate alone, would Polybius still call the resulting system "mixed"? What would be lost?

assignments.title: 1.21 VR Sync Activity: The Roman Senate House, Debating the Dual Executive
assignments.html:
Setting: the Roman Senate House (Curia). Time: ~30 minutes. Category: Synchronous Homework and Activities.

This activity works whether you attend a live VR class session or complete it solo. The steps are identical either way. Enter the virtual reconstruction of the Curia. You will find two lecterns marked Consul A and Consul B and a bank of Senate seating. A posted placard at the entrance summarizes a real crisis the Roman Senate faced: a proposed grain-price law that one consul supports and the other opposes.

  1. Stand at Consul A's lectern and leave a note recording the strongest argument for the law.
  2. Walk to Consul B's lectern and leave a note recording the strongest argument against it.
  3. Sit in the Senate seating and use the whiteboard to sketch how a tribune's veto could override the outcome regardless of which consul wins.
  4. Record a short walkthrough of yourself narrating: if you were a citizen watching this debate, would you want a dual executive with veto power, or a single decisive executive? Defend your answer in under two minutes.

Submit: the recording of your walkthrough, uploaded here. If completed live, your facilitator may also ask you to briefly share your answer aloud.

Facilitator note: This is the module's featured graded VR activity. If running live, let students work the four steps independently before opening informal comparison. Do not lecture the answer, since the reflection question has no single correct position.

assignments.title: 2.23 Critical Questions
assignments.html:

questions.text: [Week 10 · SS.7.CG.3.8] According to Lesson 10.1, the President's power to make treaties and appoint federal judges requires:

A public referendum of all citizens

Article III, Section 2

Adams was occupied with military duties

questions.text: According to Lesson 5.2, which specific consequence of the Articles of Confederation's weakness does the lesson name?

answers.text: Congress successfully raised a standing national army
All states adopted identical tax codes voluntarily
The Supreme Court struck down state tariffs
States printed their own currencies and taxed each other's goods at the borders

questions.text: The Mayflower Compact's signers "covenant and combine" themselves into a "civil body politic" before landing. According to the text, whose consent creates this government?

answers.text: The signers' own
King James's
The Virginia Company's
The Church of England's

questions.text: The Virginia Plan and the New Jersey Plan primarily disagreed over:

answers.text: Whether to have a president
Whether slavery should be abolished
How states would be represented in the new Congress
Where the national capital would be located

questions.text: The Great Compromise resolved the representation dispute by:

answers.text: Adopting the New Jersey Plan unchanged
Creating a two-chamber Congress, one apportioned by population and one by equal state representation
Abolishing the Senate entirely
Giving all power to the states

questions.text: Machiavelli argued in the Discourses on Livy that quarrels between Rome's nobles and plebeians:

answers.text: Destroyed the Republic's freedom
Never actually occurred
Were resolved entirely by the Senate
Were the primary cause of Rome retaining her freedom

questions.text: According to the Tenth Amendment, powers not delegated to the United States nor prohibited to the states are reserved to:

answers.text: The President alone
The Supreme Court
The states, or to the people
The United Nations

questions.text: Madison's phrase "ambition must be made to counteract ambition" in Federalist No. 51 reflects the idea that:

answers.text: Self-interested officeholders, each guarding their own branch, end up protecting the separation of powers
Good character alone preserves the separation of powers
Ambition should be eliminated from government entirely
Only virtuous men should hold office

questions.text: The Athenian Assembly's 415 BC vote to invade Sicily, recorded by Thucydides, illustrated to the American framers the danger of:

answers.text: Too many structural checks slowing government down
An executive branch with too little power
A judiciary that refused to hear cases
A single persuasive speaker and popular enthusiasm overwhelming careful deliberation, with no structural check to slow the decision

questions.text: In Federalist No. 39, Madison argued the proposed Constitution was:

answers.text: Purely national, replacing the states entirely
A composition of both federal and national elements
Purely federal, identical to the Articles of Confederation
Illegal under the Articles of Confederation

questions.text: Hamilton rejected direct popular election of the president chiefly because he worried it risked:

answers.text: Too slow a process
Excessive Senate involvement
A charismatic demagogue sweeping an emotional majority without the qualifications for office
Violating the Necessary and Proper Clause

questions.text: According to Aristotle's Politics, Book V, revolutions are most often caused by:

answers.text: A shared sense among some group that it lacks its rightful share of honor, office, or power
Foreign invasion alone
Excessive wealth equally distributed
The absence of a written constitution

questions.text: Hamilton designed electors to meet "in the State in which they are chosen," rather than all together, chiefly to:

answers.text: Save travel costs
Prevent small states from voting at all
Guarantee unanimous outcomes
Reduce the "heats and ferments" that mass gatherings can produce

questions.text: According to Lesson 3.2, the Senate's staggered six-year terms were designed to:

answers.text: Match the House's rapid turnover exactly
Be insulated enough from immediate public pressure to deliberate more slowly than the House
Prevent the Senate from ever changing membership
Eliminate the need for elections

questions.text: The doctrine that a national legislature may exercise only the powers specifically granted to it in the constitutional text is called:

answers.text: Federalism
Judicial review
Enumerated powers
Separation of powers

questions.text: According to Article V, a proposed constitutional amendment becomes valid once ratified by:

answers.text: Three-fourths of the states, by legislature or convention
A simple majority of Congress alone
Unanimous consent of all fifty states
The President's signature alone

questions.text: John Adams's Massachusetts Constitution describes a "government of laws, and not of men" as achieved by:

answers.text: A single branch holding legislative, executive, and judicial power together
Direct popular vote on every law
Abolishing all courts
Keeping the legislative, executive, and judicial powers permanently separate

questions.text: According to Lesson 3.18, the President's power to make treaties and appoint federal judges requires:

answers.text: The Advice and Consent of the Senate
A public referendum of all citizens
Approval from the Supreme Court
A unanimous vote of the House

questions.text: According to Lesson 3.22, the presidential veto is textually located in:

answers.text: Article II, Section 1
Article III, Section 2
The Bill of Rights
Article I, Section 7, not Article II

questions.text: Hamilton names two reasons for the presidential veto in Federalist No. 73. Which pair correctly matches his own ranking?

answers.text: Primary: protecting the community; secondary: letting the President defend himself
Primary: letting the President defend himself; secondary: protecting the community against bad laws
Both reasons are equally primary, with no ranking
Neither reason concerns the legislature at all

questions.text: According to Lesson 3.31, federal judges hold office "during good Behaviour" chiefly so that:

answers.text: Congress can replace them easily
They can serve on multiple courts at once
A judge who feared losing the job would not be a genuinely independent check on the other branches
They never need Senate confirmation

questions.text: According to Lesson 3.31, federal courts may:

answers.text: Only hear cases falling within specific categories named in Article III, Section 2
Choose to rule on any dispute they find interesting
Only hear cases involving the President
Never review acts of Congress

questions.text: Hamilton calls the judiciary "the least dangerous" branch in Federalist No. 78 because, unlike Congress and the President, it:

answers.text: Has the fewest members
Rarely hears real cases
Cannot ever be checked by the other branches
Commands neither the power of the purse nor the power of the sword, only judgment

questions.text: According to Lesson 4.2, the Bill of Rights is best understood as:

answers.text: A grant of brand-new freedoms from a generous government
A fence marking territory the government may not enter, not a grant of new freedoms
A list of duties citizens owe the government
A replacement for the original Constitution

questions.text: The First Amendment's opening phrase, "Congress shall make no law," tells you the amendment directly restrains:

answers.text: Private citizens
State governments only
The national legislature
Foreign governments

questions.text: According to Lesson 4.6, the Supreme Court's 2008 ruling in District of Columbia v. Heller held that the Second Amendment protects:

answers.text: An individual right to keep a firearm for lawful purposes, unconnected with militia service
A right that exists only for members of an organized state militia
No right at all, since the amendment was ruled obsolete
A right that only Congress, not individuals, may exercise

questions.text: According to Lesson 4.11, a government action touching religion satisfies the Lemon test only if it:

answers.text: Has any purpose Congress considers reasonable
Directly funds a specific religious denomination
Avoids all mention of religion in any statute
Has a secular purpose, neither advances nor inhibits religion as its primary effect, and avoids excessive government entanglement with religion

questions.text: The Pennsylvania and Rhode Island laws struck down in Lemon v. Kurtzman had used state funds to:

answers.text: Build new public schools
Pay religious school teachers' salaries for secular subjects
Fund a national church
Ban religious schools entirely

questions.text: According to Lesson 4.15, once a law substantially burdens someone's free exercise of religion, the Sherbert test requires the government to show:

answers.text: That a majority of citizens support the law
Only that the law applies equally to everyone
A "compelling state interest" justifying the burden
Nothing further, since free exercise claims automatically fail

questions.text: According to Lesson 4.20, Miranda warnings are legally required only when a suspect is:

answers.text: In police custody and about to be questioned to draw out incriminating information
Asked any question at all by any officer, custody or not
Formally charged in court
Released on bail

questions.text: According to Lesson 4.24, Terry v. Ohio permits a brief stop and pat-down for weapons based on:

answers.text: A formal warrant
Probable cause identical to the standard for a full arrest
Anonymous tips alone, with no officer observation required
"Reasonable suspicion," supported by specific and articulable facts, a lower standard than probable cause

questions.text: A student claims the Miranda ruling found Ernesto Miranda factually innocent of the crime he was accused of. Based on Lesson 4.20, is this accurate?

answers.text: Yes
No: the ruling concerned the constitutionality of how his confession was obtained, not his factual guilt or innocence
Yes, and he was awarded damages
No, because the Court refused to hear his case

questions.text: According to Lesson 4.29, the Supreme Court's ruling in Brown v. Board of Education held that segregated schools were:

answers.text: Equal so long as funding was matched
A matter for each state legislature to decide, not the courts
Inherently unequal, regardless of whether resources were formally matched
Constitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment

questions.text: According to Lesson 4.33, Homer Plessy's boarding of the railway car reserved for white passengers was:

answers.text: A deliberately staged test case arranged in advance with the railroad's cooperation
A spontaneous, unplanned act of civil disobedience
An accident, since Plessy did not know the law existed
Ordered by the state government itself

questions.text: In his lone dissent in Plessy v. Ferguson, Justice Harlan wrote that:

answers.text: Segregation should be decided by popular vote
The federal government had no authority over state railway law
"Separate but equal" was an efficient solution
"Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens"

questions.text: According to Lesson 5.2, the Sixth Amendment's guarantee of an impartial jury depends on:

answers.text: Judges selecting their own juries
Ordinary citizens actually showing up to serve when summoned
Professional lawyers volunteering their time
The President appointing jurors directly

questions.text: According to Lesson 5.6, the 1863 Civil War draft allowed a drafted man to avoid service by:

answers.text: Enlisting in the Navy instead
Serving only within his home state
Paying a $300 commutation fee or hiring a substitute
Registering as a conscientious objector

questions.text: Roosevelt's December 8, 1941, address asked Congress to formally declare that a state of war existed, rather than declaring war himself, because:

answers.text: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress, not the President, the power to declare war
The Constitution required a unanimous Cabinet vote first
Congress alone could raise a militia under the Second Amendment
Roosevelt lacked the authority to command the armed forces

questions.text: According to Lesson 5.12, the policy of "containment," first announced in the Truman Doctrine, aimed to:

answers.text: Merge the U.S. and Soviet economies
Roll back Soviet communism by force wherever it existed
Withdraw the U.S. from all foreign commitments
Prevent the further spread of Soviet communism, without necessarily reversing it where it already existed

questions.text: NATO's core promise, according to Lesson 5.12, is that:

answers.text: All members must adopt identical governments
An attack on any member is treated as an attack on all
Only the United States may act militarily
Members may not trade with non-members

questions.text: According to Lesson 5.16, President George H.W. Bush's response to the 1990 invasion of Kuwait differed from Truman's approach chiefly in that Bush:

answers.text: Acted entirely alone, without allies
Refused to involve the United Nations
Built a multinational coalition through UN Security Council resolutions rather than confronting a single rival superpower alone
Declared containment obsolete and adopted rollback instead

questions.text: According to Lesson 5.22, the 1932–1933 Soviet famine was largely caused by:

answers.text: State grain-requisition policy, not primarily natural disaster
An unusually severe drought with no government role
A foreign military blockade
Peasant farmers withholding their own grain for profit

questions.text: According to Lesson 5.22, Gareth Jones's reporting mattered because he:

answers.text: Repeated the official Soviet denial of any famine
Wrote his account from inside the Kremlin
Focused only on Soviet industrial achievements
Personally visited villages outside official press tours and directly contradicted the Soviet government's denial

questions.text: According to Lesson 5.26, the Gulag system was able to operate at such scale largely because the Soviet Union lacked:

answers.text: A written constitution of any kind
An independent judiciary and a free press capable of checking the state
Any prisons or courts whatsoever
A standing army

questions.text: The Olive Branch Petition modeled a civic problem-solving process that involved identifying the proper authority, stating the grievance clearly, and:

answers.text: Declaring independence immediately
Organizing a military response first
Proposing a specific resolution the authority could grant
Appealing directly to a foreign government instead

questions.text: Comparing the U.S. and Florida constitutions' preambles, the Extension reading explains that Florida's constitution:

answers.text: Can grant Floridians rights beyond what the federal Constitution requires, but cannot take away any federal constitutional right
Can override any federal constitutional right it chooses
Has no preamble of its own
Must be identical in wording to the U.S. Constitution

questions.text: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 stated that "schools and the means of education shall forever be encouraged" because the framers judged them:

answers.text: A purely private matter with no government interest
A federal responsibility only
Unnecessary for good government
Necessary to good government and the happiness of mankind

questions.text: The 12th Amendment rewrote the electoral process after the 1800 election specifically to prevent:

answers.text: States from having unequal numbers of electors
A tie between a party's own presidential and vice-presidential candidates, as happened between Jefferson and Burr
Electors from meeting in separate states
Congress from ever counting electoral votes
